step1_summary: Chief complaint: 3-day history of severe diarrhoea and vomiting

Symptoms: • Onset 3 days ago, watery initially now very loose; “lost count,” ≥4 BMs today • Subjective high fever (“literally boiling”) but no documented temperature • Repeated vomiting – unable to keep down food, water, ORS • Periumbilical abdominal pain that comes in waves with urge to pass stool • No blood in stool or urine, no rash • Last vomit ~2 h before call • Voiding urine; last urination 1 h ago; colour unknown
Aggravating/Alleviating: Nothing helps; ORS taken 3×/day for 2 days without benefit; tiny sips suggested by doctor
Past medical history: None significant; only occasional menstrual cramps; no prior GI disease or surgery
Medications/allergies: Takes vitamin D daily; occasional ibuprofen; no regular Rx; no allergies mentioned

Family/social: Brother has identical symptoms; reports school outbreak; lives with brother & mother; works as graphic designer; non-smoker; occasional alcohol; no recreational drugs; not sexually active; last period 2 weeks ago
Vital signs/exam: Remote visit – no vitals. Subjective fever, abdominal tenderness around umbilicus on palpation
Labs/imaging: None done yet; stool culture planned

V: Mesenteric ischemia: Acute abdominal pain, diarrhoea/vomiting possible, but rare in young healthy patient
I: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus): Sudden onset, family cluster, watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever
Bacterial gastroenteritis / food-borne infection (Campylobacter, Salmonella, E. coli): Similar presentation; may need stool culture
Clostridioides difficile colitis: Profuse diarrhoea, but no recent antibiotics
N: Colorectal malignancy with obstruction & overflow diarrhoea: Unlikely given age/acute course
D: Lactase deficiency / food intolerance: Could cause loose stools, but not acute febrile illness
I2: Drug-induced gastritis/enteritis from NSAIDs: Occasional ibuprofen use makes this unlikely
C: Congenital enzyme deficiency (e.g., sucrase–isomaltase): Chronic diarrhoea, not acute
A: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/UC): Can flare with diarrhoea & pain, but first episode at 38 y and infectious contact argues against
T: Abdominal trauma causing bowel injury: No history
E: Diabetic ketoacidosis or thyrotoxicosis: Vomiting possible but no other supportive features

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Sudden onset watery diarrhoea, prominent vomiting, low-grade fever, household contact with identical illness, typical 2–3 day course for norovirus.
Presentation compatible with Campylobacter, Salmonella or toxigenic E. coli; stool culture warranted because symptoms not improving after 3 days and patient febrile.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Food-borne toxin–mediated illness (Staph aureus, Bacillus cereus)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can present with abrupt vomiting and diarrhoea but usually resolves within 24 h; persistence to day 3 makes this less likely.
Diarrhoea and abdominal pain possible, but acute familial clustering, absence of blood and prior history make IBD less probable.
Periumbilical pain & vomiting fit early appendicitis, but predominant diarrhoea and lack of localized RLQ tenderness argue against.

supporting_evidence: Low-grade fever common in viral GE
opposing_evidence: Persisting beyond typical 48 h window (now day 3)
Subjectively ‘very high’ fever could suggest bacterial cause

supporting_evidence: Fever, abdominal pain, persistent symptoms past 72 h
Doctor considering stool culture for bacteria
opposing_evidence: No blood or mucus in stool reported
Symptoms usually self-limited <24 h; patient still unwell at 72 h
Family member sick for several days—spread person-to-person uncommon with pre-formed toxin
No blood, chronicity, weight loss, or prior episodes
Family infectious exposure explains illness better
Pain not localized to RLQ; no rebound/guarding assessed
